\chapter{Where Two Words Melt Into One}
\label{ch:fr-contractions}
\hlchaptermodality{39}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say to, at, of and from, and I know which four combinations of preposition and article melt into a single word.}

Every noun the book owns is put in somebody's hands and put somewhere. Two prepositions and four articles make eight combinations, four of which melt -- and the rule that decides which is the one du already showed: le and les contract, la and l' do not. The u inside au was an l, which is the same eight-century-old change that made chevaux out of cheval.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[à]{à — one letter, and the accent that saves it}

\label{lesson:FR-C35-a}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{il a} and \textbf{il y a}. The \textbf{a} in both is the verb. This lesson takes the other one.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} two chapters back, the three question words you took last — \emph{comment}, \emph{combien}, \emph{pourquoi}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{à} — to, at.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{à Paris} — to Paris, in Paris. · \textbf{à trois heures} — at three o'clock.
\end{quote}

Latin \textbf{ad} gave it, and the \textbf{d} wore off, leaving a single letter. English kept the same \emph{ad} in a hundred borrowed words — \emph{advance}, \emph{admit}, \emph{adhere} — where it still means \emph{toward}.

The grave accent has one job and no other: it separates this word from \textbf{a}, the verb. Same letter, same sound, and only the mark on the page says which is meant. French does this three times over — \emph{a}/\emph{à}, \emph{ou}/\emph{où}, \emph{la}/\emph{là} — and you have already met the third.

You have owned the clock since it was taught and had no way to say \textbf{at} a time. Now you have one.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the two \emph{a}s — the verb \textquotedblleft{}il a\textquotedblright{}, the preposition \textquotedblleft{}à Paris\textquotedblright{}
  \item the clock, at last — \textquotedblleft{}à trois heures\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}à midi\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}à minuit\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three pairs the accent separates — \textquotedblleft{}a/à\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}ou/où\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}la/là\textquotedblright{}
  \item ask for a time, then answer — \textquotedblleft{}Quelle heure est-il ? — À midi.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three modals, each pointed at a time — \textquotedblleft{}Je veux partir à midi. Je peux partir à midi. Je dois partir à midi.\textquotedblright{} — and the second verb never moving
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin word is \textbf{à}? (\emph{\textbf{Ad}}.) What is the accent for? (\textbf{To separate it from \emph{a}, the verb} — nothing else.) Say \textquotedblleft{}at midday\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}at three o'clock.\textquotedblright{}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[de]{de — \textquotedblleft{}of,\textquotedblright{} and the word already hiding in \emph{du}}

\label{lesson:FR-C35-de}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{du pain}. You were told two words are inside it. Name them.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{de} — of, from.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{le café de Paris} — the café of Paris. · \textbf{le frère de Marie} — Marie's brother.
\end{quote}

That second line is worth a moment. French owns nothing with an apostrophe: it says \textbf{the brother of Marie}, and it has said so since Latin. English is the odd one here — the possessive \textbf{'s} is a Germanic survival that Latin's daughters never had, so \emph{Marie's brother} is the outlier and \emph{le frère de Marie} is the ordinary European shape.

Before a vowel it elides, exactly as \emph{le} does:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{le livre d'Anne} — Anne's book.
\end{quote}

And you have been saying \textbf{de} since the food chapter without meeting it alone: \emph{du pain} is \textbf{de} + \textbf{le}, and \emph{de l'eau} is \textbf{de} with nothing to contract.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item possession, the French way — \textquotedblleft{}le frère de Marie\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}la mère de Anne\textquotedblright{}
  \item elided — \textquotedblleft{}le café d'Anne\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two you already had — \textquotedblleft{}du pain\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}de l'eau\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}à Paris\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}de Paris\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does French say \textquotedblleft{}Marie's brother\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Le frère de Marie} — of Marie.) Which language invented the apostrophe possessive? (\textbf{English}, and none of Latin's daughters has one.) What two words are inside \emph{du}? (\emph{\textbf{De}} and \emph{\textbf{le}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[au, aux]{au, aux — where \emph{à} and \emph{le} melt together}

\label{lesson:FR-C35-au-aux}



\begin{quote}
\emph{De} plus \emph{le} gave you \textbf{du}. Predict what \emph{à} plus \emph{le} gives before you read on.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{au} = \textbf{à} + \textbf{le}. · \textbf{aux} = \textbf{à} + \textbf{les}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{au café} — to the café. · \textbf{aux cafés} — to the cafés.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{à la maison} — no contraction, because \emph{la} is not \emph{le}.
\end{quote}

Two of the four combinations melt and two do not, and the split is the same one \emph{du} already showed you: \textbf{le} and \textbf{les} contract, \textbf{la} and \textbf{l'} stay apart.

The \emph{u} in \textbf{au} was an \emph{l}. French turned \textbf{al} into \textbf{au} across the whole language, and once you have seen it you find it everywhere:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{older shape} & \textbf{modern} \\
\midrule
\emph{bel} & \textbf{beau} \\
\emph{cheval} & \textbf{chevaux} \\
\emph{journal} & \textbf{journaux} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So the \textbf{x} on \emph{aux} and the \emph{x} on \emph{chevaux} are the same story, and a plural that looks irregular is an \emph{l} that turned into a \emph{u} eight centuries ago.

The \textbf{x} of \emph{aux} is silent alone and comes back as a \textbf{z} before a vowel — \emph{aux amis} is \emph{oh-ZAH-mee}, the liaison you have had since the numbers.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the four — \textquotedblleft{}au café\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}aux cafés\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}à la maison\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}à l'eau\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair that melt the same way — \textquotedblleft{}du café\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}au café\textquotedblright{}
  \item the liaison — \textquotedblleft{}aux amis\textquotedblright{}, \emph{oh-ZAH-mee}
  \item the \emph{l} that became a \emph{u} — \textquotedblleft{}bel, beau; cheval, chevaux\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{au} made of? (\emph{\textbf{À}} plus \emph{\textbf{le}}.) And \emph{aux}? (\emph{\textbf{À}} plus \emph{\textbf{les}}.) Which two never contract? (\emph{\textbf{La}} and \emph{\textbf{l'}}.) What was the \emph{u} of \emph{au} before it was a \emph{u}? (\textbf{An \emph{l}}, the same one inside \emph{chevaux}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[de la]{de la — the half of the partitive that was missing}

\label{lesson:FR-C35-de-la}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}some bread\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}some water\textquotedblright{}. Both are yours. Now try \textquotedblleft{}some milk\textquotedblright{} — \emph{le lait} is a \emph{le}-word, but \textbf{la viande}, meat, is not.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{de la} — some, in front of a \emph{la}-word.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{du lait} — some milk. · \textbf{de la viande} — some meat. · \textbf{de l'eau} — some water.
\end{quote}

Three shapes, one rule, and it is a rule you already own from two other places: \textbf{de} plus the article, contracting only where \emph{le} and \emph{les} contract.

That is worth stating plainly, because it looks like three separate things to memorise and is one:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the noun takes} & \textbf{some…} \\
\midrule
\emph{le} & \textbf{du} \\
\emph{la} & \textbf{de la} \\
\emph{l'} & \textbf{de l'} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The food chapter taught the first and third and stopped, because every noun on its table happened to be a \emph{le}-word or a vowel-word. The middle line was never missing from the language, only from the table.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three shapes — \textquotedblleft{}du lait, de la viande, de l'eau\textquotedblright{}
  \item the table you already had — \textquotedblleft{}du pain, du vin, du fromage\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two drinks — \textquotedblleft{}du café, du thé\textquotedblright{}
  \item article first, then the partitive — \textquotedblleft{}le lait $\to$ du lait\textquotedblright{}
  \item pointed at, then measured — \textquotedblleft{}ce lait\textquotedblright{}, then \textquotedblleft{}du lait\textquotedblright{}; \textquotedblleft{}cette eau\textquotedblright{}, then \textquotedblleft{}de l'eau\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which shape goes with a \emph{la}-word? (\emph{\textbf{De la}}.) With a \emph{le}-word? (\emph{\textbf{Du}}.) Why does \emph{de la} not contract? (\textbf{Only \emph{le} and \emph{les} ever contract} — the same rule behind \emph{du} and \emph{au}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[des]{des — the plural of \emph{un}, and the last shape of \emph{some}}

\label{lesson:FR-C35-des}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{un café} is \emph{a café}. Say the plural. English drops the word entirely — \emph{cafés} — and French cannot.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{des} — some; and the plural of \textbf{un} and \textbf{une}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{un café $\to$ des cafés} · \textbf{une amie $\to$ des amies}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Il y a des cafés.} — There are cafés.
\end{quote}

\textbf{des} is \textbf{de} + \textbf{les}, contracted exactly as \emph{du} is \emph{de} + \emph{le}. So it completes two systems at once and adds no new machinery to either.

Here English is the language with the hole. English has \emph{a} and no plural of it, so it says \emph{books}, \emph{cafés}, \emph{friends} with nothing in front. French will not leave the slot empty, and a sentence with a bare plural noun in it sounds unfinished to a French ear. That is the single commonest mistake an English speaker makes in French, and it is a missing word rather than a wrong one.

The \textbf{s} is silent, and it comes back as a \textbf{z} before a vowel: \emph{des amies} is \emph{day-ZAH-mee}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item singular then plural — \textquotedblleft{}un café, des cafés\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}un chien, des chiens; un chat, des chats\textquotedblright{}
  \item the liaison — \textquotedblleft{}des amies\textquotedblright{}, \emph{day-ZAH-mee}
  \item existence and identity, in the plural — \textquotedblleft{}Il y a des cafés.\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}Ce sont des amis.\textquotedblright{}
  \item all four shapes of \emph{some} — \textquotedblleft{}du, de la, de l', des\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two words are inside \emph{des}? (\emph{\textbf{De}} and \emph{\textbf{les}}.) What is the plural of \emph{un café}? (\emph{\textbf{Des cafés}}.) What does English put in that slot? (\textbf{Nothing} — it has no plural of \emph{a}.) Say all four shapes of \emph{some}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Au café — the chapter, run cold}

\label{lesson:FR-R35-au-cafe}



\begin{quote}
Two prepositions and four articles make eight combinations. Four melt into one word and four do not. Say which four melt, and say the one rule that decides it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn: the four that melt}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{à} melting — \textquotedblleft{}au café\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}aux cafés\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{de} melting — \textquotedblleft{}du pain\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}des amis\textquotedblright{}
  \item the four that stay apart — \textquotedblleft{}à la maison\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}à l'eau\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}de la viande\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}de l'eau\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two liaisons — \textquotedblleft{}aux amis\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}des amis\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: the distant band — everything, placed and possessed}
Every noun the book owns, put in somebody's hands and put somewhere.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the table, possessed — \textquotedblleft{}le pain de Marie, le vin de Paris, le café d'Anne\textquotedblright{}
  \item the table, in the plural — \textquotedblleft{}des œufs, des cafés, du sel, du sucre, du beurre\textquotedblright{}
  \item the household, possessed — \textquotedblleft{}la mère de Marie, le frère d'Anne, la sœur de Paul\textquotedblright{}
  \item the animals — \textquotedblleft{}le chien de l'enfant, le chat de l'ami\textquotedblright{}
  \item the clock, at last with a preposition — \textquotedblleft{}à midi\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}à minuit\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}à trois heures\textquotedblright{}
  \item put it all together — \textquotedblleft{}Il y a des cafés là-bas. C'est le café de Marie. Je suis au café.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two articles contract, and which two never do? (\emph{\textbf{Le}} and \emph{\textbf{les}} contract; \emph{\textbf{la}} and \emph{\textbf{l'}} do not.) Name the four melted words. (\emph{\textbf{Au, aux, du, des}}.) How does French say \textquotedblleft{}Marie's bread\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Le pain de Marie}.) And what does English have that French does not need? (\textbf{An apostrophe.})
\end{tcolorbox}
